items.title: Lew Soloff interviewed by Monk Rowe, Scottsdale, Arizona, April 16, 2000
items.q: And I was lucky enough to work with Gil for a long period of time, and I was lucky enough to experience what he was like as a band leader

ctx.x: You stated in a recent liner note that Gil Evans’ gig was the greatest one you’ve done. Does that still hold up?

Sure it does. He was, I mean him and Dizzy were the two, to me, two absolute geniuses. And I was lucky enough to work with Gil for a long period of time, and I was lucky enough to experience what he was like as a band leader, which was basically never telling you what to play, maybe giving you a little hint maybe once a year. But basically never telling you what or how to play and just using you, or having you in his musical organization, as long as you played the way he liked. In other words he picked his…
Wow. That’s saying a lot. You said that you started on the trumpet because it was shiny?

items.title: 66960_Gil Evans oral history interview
items.q: Lou Soloff (I couldn't do without Dave really?). You the First trumpet player. He's with Blood Sweat and Tears too. But he flew down to play that concert with me that afternoon

ctx.x: Well I think he did it at least three times.

How about that. And I have to have a trombone player from the, he's now playing at the Blood, Sweat, and Tears too, he's name is Dave Bargerom (Bargerou?). Now he came from a musical, theatrical family from New England. They had a troupe, I guess the (Bargerou?) family were like a troupe. They played vaudeville a long time ago. Dave was raised in that kind of thing. So it shows in his solos, you know. Sometimes he'll play like a real 1920 style trombone. He heard it playing on records at his parents house. And…
